newsitem.title: THAILAND: INTERVIEW - Thais aim to boost sugar productivity.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Thais aim to boost sugar productivity.

text.p: Thailand aims to improve sugar productivity for the 1997/98 season (November-October) by introducing new strains, providing irrigation support and improving management, a senior industry ministry official said.

Pramote Vidtayasuk, secretary general of Thai Cane and Sugar board, told Reuters that the sugar output for 1997/98 was expected to be slightly higher than the current season's but the plantation area would not be expanded.

"We have not come up with the forecast for 1997/98 yet as we are still assessing the situation. It seems some cassava farmers could switch to sugar cane. Anyway, we believe it will be slightly higher than 1996/97," he said.
"The aim for this year would be for the industry to inprove its productivity without having to increase the acreage," Pramote added.

The preliminary figure of sugar production this season was 5.795 million tonnes tel quel, according to industry ministry officials. This is well below the earlier projection of 6.28 million tonnes due to lower-than-expected sugar cane output.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) forecast put Thailand's sugar output at 6.36 million tonnes raw value compared with 6.25 tonnes estimated in 1996/97.

It also projected world production at 122.4 million tonnes and the consumption at a record 125 million tonnes due to a mix of factors including higher consumer incomes, population growth and rising demand for sugar products such as soft drinks and processed foods.
Pramote said the government was introducing three new higher yielding strains to farmers which should help increase the output by at least 10 percent.
"These new breeds yield around 87-93 tonnes of sugar cane per hectare in the experimental plantation. They are also more resistant to disease," he said.

"But there are certain limitations. We don't expect the strains to yield this high in every plantation as it depends on weather and the amount of water as well. The new breeds might be suitable to the central region only," he added.

Pramote said the board would also encourage more mechanical cutting as labour costs were soaring and he vowed to cultivate better cooperation between the mills and the farmers during the crushing season in order to boost productivity and reduce costs.
